items.title: Will the AI stock sell-off give us sub-7% mortgage rates before the holidays?
items.description: Sub-7% mortgage rates are back on the holiday menu! Just when it looked like we had no chance for a happy holiday, AI stocks are still taking a beating and pushing money into bonds. Oil prices almost went below $80 last week too. We have three holidays left before 2027 kicks into gear, so the question now is: Can we get the 10-year yield and mortgage spreads low enough to get lower mortgage rates ? 10-year yield and mortgage rates In the 2026 HousingWire forecast , I anticipated the following ranges: Mortgage rates between 5.75% and 6.75% The 10-year yield fluctuating between 3.80% and 4.60% If all this market drama happened four weeks ago, I believe the 10-year yield would be under 4.85% today, but this is happening amid a rapid-fire, two-week effort by the Federal Reserve to give forward-guidance about more rate hikes coming in the system. The key level of 5.15% for the 10-year yield held last week, and with the AI sell-off and oil prices down to $83 again, we have a shot to get sub-7% mortgage rates again, but that will require the 10-year yield to get to 4.85% and head lower — and for mortgage spreads to improve back down toward 2%. Mortgage rates have had a difficult time lately with the inflation data and the Fed's hawkish tone. In addition, we still don’t have a resolution to the Iran conflict, and when President Trump talks about bigger tariffs with our partners, it makes it harder for yields to go down. We also have to be mindful that inflation is rising while the unemployment rate is falling; if those two things change, it will be better for rates. For now, let’s focus on getting rates lower before the holidays. What can get us there? 1. Stocks selling off almost got us to 4.85% again; we got as low as 4.92% Friday. The problem is the speed of the decline doesn’t help mortgage spreads. However, if we see more market selling, that can be one positive variable. 2. Any positive news on the Iran conflict or limiting the trade war. 3. The hope that the Democrats will resolve the conflict and trade war after Jan. 3 might get bond traders and oil traders thinking differently. We don’t have much time before the end-of-year holidays, but the above will help. However, the reverse is also true: stocks rallying, the conflict getting worse or more negative trade war headlines can lead yields and rates higher. Mortgage spreads Mortgage spreads have recently gotten worse, which is a big variable in why rates got as high as 7.60% recently, but they’re still close to multiyear lows. We need less volatility in the bond markets, and with time, the spreads can improve again. Since September, the markets have been a bit too wild, rising and falling, and the spreads' job is to reduce mortgage rate volatility. A big key for mortgage rates to get below 7% is getting the spreads back to 2% and under. Historically, mortgage spreads have ranged from 1.60% to 1.80%. Last week, spreads rose to 2.18% from 2.15% a week earlier. Let’s compare last week’s mortgage rates to where they would have been at the best spread levels this year and the worst levels of this cycle. If we had the best levels of spreads in 2026, mortgage rates would be 6.96% today, not 7.33% . If we had the worst mortgage spread levels of 2023, mortgage rates would be 8.26% today. Weekly pending sales Our pending home sales data provides a week-to-week perspective, though holidays and short-term fluctuations can affect results. This weekly pending sales data typically takes 30-60 days to reflect in sales data. We saw slight week-to-week growth last week and housing data has really stabilized in the recent weeks; however, I would just view this as an adjustment to the rate shock we saw when rates moved from 6.75% to 7.60%, and demand got noticeably hit. The year-over-year comps are going to be difficult for some time, as mortgage rates were much lower last year than today. Here are the pending sales for last week over the last two years: 2026: 53,490 2025: 58,612 Purchase applications Purchase application data, which looks out 30-90 days, has softened as mortgage rates rose above 6.64% and are now above 7%. Rates rose aggressively during inflation week, so this data line did get hit, down 3% week-to-week and down 18% year-over-year. Again, the year-over-year comps here are rough, as mortgage rates were a lot lower last year. Earlier in the year, all we had was positive year-over-year, but rates reached the range where housing data slows down, and the comps have been very difficult. Here are the stats on purchase apps so far in 2026: 17 positive week-to-week prints 25 negative week-to-week prints 5 flat week-to-week prints 10 weeks of double-digit year-over-year growth 25 weeks of positive year-over-year growth 17 negative year-over-year prints Housing inventory Housing inventory had a slight decline last week and is in its seasonal decline for 2026, as the peak in inventory already happened. Inventory growth did pick up when mortgage rates headed toward 7.60%; before that, inventory growth was slow this year, and we even had some weeks when inventory was negative year-over-year. Until mid-June it was hard for the comps to show growth this year and now they’re much easier to show growth as housing demand was heading toward a nine-month high last year this time. items.description: HighlightsThe vacancy rate in the Kansas City build-to-rent (BTR) market has declined in each of the past two quarters. Deliveries have slowed, with projects totaling roughly 325 units being completed year to date. In 2025, approximately 800 units came online.Despite a dip during the third quarter, asking rents in the BTR sector rose 3% in the past year to $2,153 per month. Current asking rents for BTR properties are exceeding traditional apartment rents by more than $850 per month while trailing the average monthly mortgage payment on a median-priced home by roughly $1,000 per month.After reaching nearly 9% at the start of 2026, vacancy has trended lower in back-to-back quarters. During the past three months, the vacancy rate declined by 30 basis points to 8.1%. Year over year, vacancy is down 10 basis points.Sales activity for build-to-rent properties has been steady in 2026, with one BTR transaction being recorded in each quarter. In transactions where pricing was available, the median price to this point in 2026 is $161,100 per unit. In 2025, the median price was $257,100 per unit.Kansas City build-to-rent market overviewSupply growth in the Kansas City build-to-rent sector continues, but at a slower rate. After more than 1,000 units came online in 2023, annual deliveries totaled 550 units in 2024 and then nearly 800 units in 2025. Construction will be lower this year, with approximately 500 units slated for delivery. Lighter and more consistent delivery levels have caused the vacancy outlook to brighten. While the overall rate remains elevated, vacancy has trended lower by 70 basis points during the past six months. Additionally, the sector posted a year-over-year vacancy improvement for the first time in nearly two years. Supply growth in 2027 is expected to track levels recorded in 2026. There are an additional 1,250 units being planned or proposed, but these projects will likely begin to enter the market in 2028 at the earliest.Following a strong close to the year in 2025, which included Sallee Development’s portfolio sale and several other transactions, the pace of BTR sales in Kansas City has slowed. Transactions in recent years have included a mix of townhomes and properties consisting of detached, traditional homes. Year to date, every BTR property that has changed hands has been a townhome community. That is not the only shift to occur in recent periods, as investors have pivoted from Missouri to Kansas. To this point in the year, nearly every sale has occurred in Kansas. Prior to this year, BTR transactions had been dominated by properties located in Missouri. Cap rates have continued to average roughly 5% since the beginning of 2025.Construction:Roughly 600 units are currently under construction. Projects totaling more than 1,250 units were in the planning phases at the end of the third quarter.Vacancy:Vacancy is down 10 basis points year over year. Vacancy declined by 30 basis points during the third quarter to 8.1%.Following the recent tightening, vacancy among BTR properties is now down 10 basis points year over year. This marks the first annual vacancy improvement since the end of 2024.Following increases throughout 2025 and into early 2026, vacancies have begun to level off in recent periods. The vacancy rate declined by a combined 70 basis points during the past six months, marking the first time since 2022 that vacancy has declined in consecutive quarters.Rents:Rents are up 3% from one year ago. items.title: Anthropic IPO vs. U.S. Housing Wealth
items.description: Anthropic IPO vs. U.S. Housing Wealth By Anthony Smith Nov 19, 2026 A Golden, Golden Gate Bridge Getty Images Anthropic IPO vs. U.S. Housing Wealth – A $1.494 Trillion IPO, Measured in Houses Anthropic's IPO Valuation Tops the Value of Every Owner-Occupied Home in San Francisco Highlights: Bigger than the San Francisco market. Priced at $83 a share, above its $70 to $78 range, Anthropic's fully diluted valuation of about $1.494 trillion clears the $1.371 trillion of owner-occupied homes across the San Francisco metro by $123 billion. More than 46 states. The valuation exceeds the total value of owner-occupied homes in 46 of 50 individual states (as well as DC), and in 391 of 393 metros. It equals about 3.4% of the $43.6 trillion in owner-occupied homes nationwide. Room left over. Every home for sale in the 50 states would come in around roughly $820 billion in October 2026. Even if we round up to $850 billion, the valuation could cover all of it and still have more than $640 billion to spare. Anthropic's initial public offering (IPO) priced Wednesday at $83 a share, above its $70 to $78 range, and the stock is set to begin trading Thursday on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT. The company sold 980 million Class A shares, raising about $81 billion. At the IPO price, its fully diluted valuation comes to roughly $1.494 trillion. It’s hard to conceptualize how large this number is, so for context, we are putting it in terms of real estate. Worth More Than Every Owner-Occupied Home in the San Francisco Metro The AI boom has reshaped the Bay Area housing market . Anthropic is headquartered in San Francisco, and owner-occupied homes across the San Francisco-Oakland-Fremont metro are worth a combined $1.371 trillion, according to the 2025 American Community Survey (ACS). Anthropic's valuation tops that by about $123 billion, a gap larger than the survey's margin of error. Only 2 metros hold more owner-occupied home value than Anthropic is worth: New York ($3.26 trillion), and Los Angeles ($2.64 trillion). The valuation equals about 46% of the New York metro's total. Within city limits, it is 1.30 times the $1.15 trillion in owner-occupied homes in New York City, however, a significant amount of New Yorkers rent, so that total leaves out the rental buildings that hold most of the city's housing. The valuation also exceeds the owner-occupied home value of 46 of 50 states, as well as DC. New Jersey comes in at $1.44 trillion, just short of the valuation estimates. Nationwide, owner-occupied homes are worth $43.6 trillion, so Anthropic's valuation equals about 3.4% of all U.S. owner-occupied housing wealth. The $494 Billion After the Trillion Set aside the first $1 trillion and Anthropic's valuation still has $494 billion left. That alone could buy every home for sale in the 20 metros with the highest total listed value: about 372,000 homes listed at a combined $356 billion, with roughly $138 billion to spare. The full valuation reaches much further. About 1.18 million homes are for sale across the US, listed at a combined $820 billion. Anthropic's valuation could cover every one of them and still have about $678 billion left. Even the Rounding Error Is Worth Billions Financial figures and data often get rounded to one or two digits, so it wouldn’t be strange to see the valuation rounded to $1.49 trillion. However, the dropped digit in $1.494 trillion is $4 billion, roughly the combined value of every owner occupied home in city of Racine, Wisconsin ($3.97 billion), or enough to buy every home for sale in the entire Raleigh-Cary, NC metro, (roughly $3.84 billion). That same $4 billion could buy every home for sale in Alaska (2,196 listings worth $1.16 billion). For when Alaska gets too cold, it could also cover every home for sale on Kauai, the Kapa’a, Hawaii, market (356 listings worth $925 million), and still leave about $1.9 billion to purchase all homes for sale in the Boulder Colorado metro area. Methodology Anthropic's valuation is the fully diluted valuation at the final IPO price of $83 per share, set Nov. 18, 2026. It uses about 18.0 billion fully diluted shares, the same share count behind the $1.405 trillion figure reported at $78. The offering was upsized to 980 million Class A shares and a separate private placement added about 313 million more, so a share count drawn from the final prospectus would run somewhat higher. Press reports round the valuation to $1.5 trillion. Owner-occupied home values come from the 2025 ACS 1-year estimates, table B25082 (aggregate value of owner-occupied housing units). ACS value is the homeowner's own estimate of what the home would sell for, not an appraisal or sale price. It excludes renter-occupied and vacant homes and all commercial property, and it reflects 2025 survey responses, while the valuation is a November 2026 market price. Comparisons described as exceeding a geography clear the upper bound of the estimate's 90% margin of error. For-sale values are the sum of list prices for active Realtor.com listings in October 2026, by state and by core-based statistical area

items.description: Nuveen Provides $227.5M C-PACE Loan for Refinancing of East Austin Office Campus by Taylor Williams November 20, 2026 November 20, 2026 6 AUSTIN, TEXAS — Nuveen Green Capital has provided a $227.5 million Commercial Property Assessed Clean Energy (C-PACE) loan for the refinancingof Springdale Green, an 881,427-square-foot office campus in East Austin. Springdale Green consists of two office buildings and a parking garage on a 30-acre site, 20 acres of which have been preserved as woodlands and walking trails. The property also features 76,800 square feet of fitness- and wellness-themed amenities, including a yoga deck, basketball, pickleball and sand volleyball courts and a multi-purpose event lawn. The sponsor is California-based Jay Paul Co., and the transaction marks the largest C-PACE loan in Texas history, according to Nuveen. items.title: Pulley raises $64 million to speed permitting and development
items.description: Pulley , a development technology company that helps multifamily and commercial development projects navigate permitting and approvals, has raised $64 million in new funding to expand its AI-driven services, the company announced this week. The financing includes a $41 million Series B round led by Jump Capital with participation from Catalyst Investors , and a $23 million Series A round led by CRV and Susa Ventures . Pulley said the capital follows 5x year-over-year growth in annual recurring revenue and will support both expansion of its permitting business and new products aimed at compressing pre-construction timelines. Pulley has partnered with multifamily developers like Wood Partners , as well as large retailers, restaurants, banks, and manufacturers, including Amazon , Starbucks , JLL and Meta . Pulley operates in entitlement, due diligence and approvals, a part of the development lifecycle that has grown increasingly complex for multifamily and commercial real estate. The company estimates that 80% of project time is now spent before construction begins, as developers navigate zoning, environmental review, design iterations and building codes that vary widely across jurisdictions. "The speed at which we build is one of the most important challenges facing America over the next decade," said Charlie Jacobson, Pulley co-founder and CEO, in the announcement. “To remain a global leader in AI, bring manufacturing back home, reach energy independence and sustain job growth, we need to build orders of magnitude faster. The single biggest lever to building faster is to get started faster." AI-assisted permitting across all 50 states Pulley said it combines AI-powered tools with a nationwide team of more than 75 licensed experts and a proprietary regulatory database to help clients secure approvals “faster and more predictably.” The company reports that it has supported $21 billion in commercial construction projects across all 50 states and thousands of cities and counties, saving customers a combined 11,750 weeks of project time. Pulley’s services include diligence, approval strategies, construction plan reviews and coordination with local agencies. The company also participates in private plan review programs, allowing it to approve building plans directly in place of local jurisdictions in more than 2,000 cities and counties, according to the announcement. The company said customers typically see just one round of comments from permitting authorities per project, and more than 40% of projects are approved without any feedback. Pulley reported that projects on its system have received 65% fewer review comments this year compared with 2025, as its models and rules engine learn from each submission. With the new funding, Pulley plans to extend beyond permitting into other pre-construction decisions that affect cost and schedule. New capabilities will combine zoning and permitting data with utility availability, local sentiment and other constraints to help owners and developers evaluate sites and programs. Pulley is also rolling out AI-assisted drawing review designed to flag building code compliance issues earlier in design, reducing redesign cycles and surprises during plan check. Why this matters for housing and construction Lengthy permitting and entitlement timelines are a major driver of project risk and carrying costs for residential and commercial developers, particularly in high-growth markets where local agencies are understaffed and regulations are changing quickly. For build-to-rent sponsors, single-family developers and multifamily owners, a slow or unpredictable approvals process can derail capital plans and delay unit delivery into tight markets. Tools that standardize and partially automate permitting, codify jurisdictional rules and centralize reviewer feedback are increasingly seen as a way to protect returns and reduce soft costs. Pulley’s growth and new capital signal continued investor interest in technology focused on the “paper side” of development rather than just construction itself, and could accelerate adoption of private plan review and AI-enabled compliance checks across more jurisdictions. items.title: Philly Life Sciences Players Say Sluggish Market Needs More VC, State Funding
items.description: The Philadelphia life sciences market is still struggling with high vacancy after some developers made speculative bets on lab space during the sector's pandemic-era boom. Bisnow/Noah Zucker Breakthrough Properties' Joe Traynor, Brandywine Realty Trust's Jeff DeVuono, Gattuso Development Partners' Janice Wong, Wexford Science & Technology's Pete Cramer, CannonDesign's Matthew Thomson and Cushman & Wakefield's Brian Young The situation could be worse, as life sciences landlords have less empty space to fill in Philly than in some other major markets. Local real estate players remain somewhat optimistic about the industry’s future, especially if a recent uptick in venture capital funding can be sustained and if the commonwealth commits more funds to the industry. “For it to get better, this region really has to focus on the growth of VC funds,” Brandywine Realty Trust Senior Managing Director of Life Science Jeff DeVuono said Wednesday during Bisnow ’s Philadelphia Life Sciences and Innovation Summit, held at the DoubleTree by Hilton Hotel Philadelphia Center City. “The governor's office has done a phenomenal job,” he added. “They brought more new companies into the commonwealth of Pennsylvania in the last four years than the state has done in the last 20. It's an incredible leadership team. Hopefully, they still have some fuel in the tank.” Greater Philly's 8.7M SF life sciences market had a 27% total vacancy rate for the first quarter of 2026, which was down just 0.2% year-over-year, according to a JLL report. The amount of unoccupied square footage pales in comparison to metro Boston, which had 33% vacancy across more than 51M SF over the same period. “Philadelphia is strong, particularly compared to Boston,” Wexford Science & Technology Vice President of Development Pete Cramer said. He said the roughly 30% rent discount that tenants can get in Philly compared to Boston is a major draw and that the general cost-of-living savings are even greater. “That’s a huge competitive advantage,” Cramer said. Philly life sciences saw about $400M in venture capital funding in Q3 2026, which was up about 25% from the same period last year, according to a Savills report. Over the first nine months of this year, the brokerage calculated $2.2B worth of VC investment in the region, already more than double the $1B total in 2025. Bisnow/Noah Zucker Monell Chemical Senses Center's Benjamin Smith, Pennsylvania Biotechnology Center's Lou Kassa, Penn Health-Tech's Katie Reuther, Children's Hospital of Philadelphia's Zev Sunleaf and Ben Franklin Technology Partners of Southeastern Pennsylvania's Scott Nissenbaum A large chunk of that came from the roughly $800M that Wilmington-based biotech firm Earendil Labs fielded in the first quarter to scale its artificial intelligence program. But leasing demand in the Philly life sciences space remains muted. “We have to approach with caution,” DeVuono said. Brandywine started tracking life sciences leasing inquiries in 2021 and found that about 80 firms were interested in the market, he said. Since then, the number has dropped to about a dozen. The industry in Philly is heavily focused on gene and cell therapy , which isn’t fielding much investment these days, DeVuono added. Much of the region's recent activity has come from biomanufacturing facilities, rather than life sciences labs. That is an area Gov. Josh Shapiro has sought to boost in Eastern Pennsylvania. He scored a series of wins on that front this year, including the $3.5B facility Eli Lilly & Co. broke ground on this month in the Lehigh Valley and the upcoming Johnson & Johnson plant in Montgomery County . “Gov. Shapiro is looking for wins, and he's gotten a lot of them,” Cushman & Wakefield Senior Director Brian Young said. “Hopefully, we can ride that wave as long as we can.” Bisnow/Noah Zucker Pennovation Works' Denita Henderson, The Wistar Institute's Peter Scarpati, B Labs' Bob Rovinsky, HDR's Eric Jaffe and Mispro's John Fogarty Both of those projects came with state incentives, but panelists said Pennsylvania needs to dole out more on that front to compete with Massachusetts and California. “As much as the cost of living is lower, there's a perception that there just aren't incentives,” Young said. There was some optimism about Innovate 2.0, a $125M fund for life sciences set aside in the commonwealth’s 2026-2027 budget. “It’s a start,” Pennsylvania Biotechnology Center CEO Lou Kassa said. “I don't know if it’s going to move the needle a whole lot.” It will be important to track the impact of that funding so the industry can effectively stump for more going forward, said Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia Vice President, Technology Transfer, Commercialization, and Research Contracts Zev Sunleaf. DeVuono predicted that up-and-coming robotics, engineering and radiopharmacology firms will soon be considering Pennsylvania. “In the next five years, you’re going to see more VC investment in Philadelphia in early-stage companies,” he said. items.description: Weekly Housing Trends: U.S. Market Update (Week Ending Nov. 14, 2026) By Anthony Smith Nov 19, 2026 Welcome to this weekly housing trends update, where we bring you the latest snapshot of inventory trends, listing activity, and buyer-seller dynamics across the U.S. housing market. In addition to our monthly housing trends reports , which offer deeper insights into long-term patterns, we publish these weekly updates to provide more timely views into market changes. This effort began in response to rapid shifts in the economy and housing landscape. You can count on a new Weekly Housing Trends update, fresh weekly data each Thursday, and a weekly video from our economists to help you stay informed. What this week’s data shows Mortgage rates remain in the lower 7% range, and both sides of the market continue to pull back. Active inventory is up 8.6% from a year ago. However, this is not because sellers are rushing in. New listings are still running below last year’s pace, and homes are taking 2 days longer to sell, the widest gap since mid-April. Sellers have kept cutting their asking prices, with the median listing price down 2.4% year over year, matching its steepest decline since early October, yet buyers have not returned in force. The latest contract data shows how deep the pullback runs. Pending home sales fell 4.7% in October to another record low and were down 16.7% from a year earlier, as mortgage rates peaked at 7.4%. Rates have since eased, but October’s hot inflation data has markets expecting a Fed rate hike in December, which could push borrowing costs higher again. For buyers who can afford to act, there is an upside with fewer shoppers meaning less competition, more homes to choose from, and sellers who are more open to negotiating on price, repairs, or closing costs. Active inventory climbed 8.6% year-over-year The number of homes for sale rose 8.6% compared to a year ago, the fourth straight week of growth at 8% or higher. Inventory has been building momentum since July, rising from roughly 2% year-over-year growth in mid-July to nearly 9% now. This pickup is not being driven by a flood of new sellers, but by a pullback in buyer activity that is letting unsold listings pile up. Year-to-date, active inventory is up 5.1%. Homes spent 2 days longer on the market compared to a year ago Median days on market came in at 66 days, with homes selling 2 days slower than the same time last year. This marks the fourth week in a row that time on market has slowed, and the widest gap since mid-April, after a long stretch reaching back to May of homes selling at the same pace or faster than last year. As mortgage rates stay above 7%, more buyers are retreating to the sidelines, and the shift could be an early signal of market slowdown. Year-to-date, time on market remains 2 days behind last year’s pace. New listings, a measure of sellers putting homes up for sale, fell 3.5% year-over-year New listing activity fell 3.5% year over year, the seventh straight week of annual declines. That is a milder drop than last week’s 10.3%, but sellers are still staying put because buyers remain disengaged. Our latest analysis of Census data found that 59% of owner-occupied homes still carry a mortgage , and owners with low-rate loans are reluctant to give up that rate for a costlier loan on their next home, which makes relocating a less attractive proposition. Year-to-date, new listings are down 0.6%. The median listing price fell 2.4% year-over-year The median listing price was $405,000, down 2.4% from the same week last year. Listing prices have now been negative on a year-over-year basis for 44 consecutive weeks. The median price per square foot also declined, falling 1.2% year over year, and the number of listings with price cuts rose 10.5%. Mortgage rates have buyers in an affordability crunch, and sellers are responding slowly. The softness is concentrated in existing homes: our latest new construction report found existing home prices 1.5% below 2025 levels in the third quarter, while new home listing prices were flat, with builders offering reduced mortgage rates to sweeten deals. Year-to-date, median listing prices sit 1.9% below 2025 levels.

items.title: Rates Jump Again as Inflation and War Worries Persist
items.description: Rates Jump Again as Inflation and War Worries Persist By Anthony Smith Nov 19, 2026 What happened to mortgage rates this week? The Freddie Mac 30-year mortgage rate jumped 17 basis points to 7.28% this week, reversing four weeks of declines that had brought rates down to 7.11%, as the 10-year Treasury yield climbed back toward 5%. Hot inflation data and the persistence of the conflict in Iran placed upward pressure on bond yields and borrowing costs. The October CPI report came in above expectations on both the headline and core measures, cementing market expectations for a December rate hike and giving the 10-year little room to fall. The debate has shifted from whether the Fed hikes in December to how aggressively it moves. That is a tough backdrop for mortgage rates heading into what is already a seasonally slow stretch for the housing market. Pending home sales fell to a record low in October , and existing home sales hit their lowest level since 2010 , as the surge in rates through mid-October took its toll on buyers and sellers alike. Builder confidence has also fallen to a 14-year low, and permit activity dropped to its lowest level since the early days of the pandemic , signaling that the supply pipeline will face continued pressure in the months ahead. What does this mean for the housing market? For buyers who remain active, conditions offer some real advantages. With fewer shoppers in the market, competition has thinned, sellers have shown more flexibility on price, and active inventory continues to rise even as new listings have pulled back. The challenge is that until inflation cools enough to put mortgage rates on a durable downward path, affordability will remain the dominant constraint on the market.

items.description: Texas Housing Insight | November 2026 Texas’ housing market continued to soften in September as rising mortgage rates, inflation, and affordability challenges restrained buyer demand, slowed sales, and kept home-price growth muted. By Yanling Mayer quick links September continued to see a pullback in market momentum, as seasonal cooling combined with rising mortgage rates, rising inflationary pressures, and affordability constraints dampened buyer activity. Existing-home sales declined from a year earlier, and market activity remained subdued. Fewer than two out of every ten homes listed for sale during the month were sold (1.5 homes), highlighting slower inventory turnover and longer marketing times amid challenging demand conditions. Year to date, sales remain modestly ahead of last year’s pace, suggesting housing demand has not deteriorated from last year. Home-price growth remained muted. Statewide home prices were essentially unchanged from a year ago, as gains in a handful of markets were offset by continued weakness elsewhere. Major metropolitan areas, including Austin, Dallas, and San Antonio, continued to experience measurable downward price pressure, while Houston and the Fort Worth metro division showed signs of modest stabilization. On the supply side, inventory levels eased seasonally following their summer peak, consistent with typical market patterns heading into the fall and winter. Nevertheless, overall inventory remains only slightly below peak summer levels, indicating that the inventory condition remains favorable to buyers. Looking ahead, the housing market is expected to remain soft through the remainder of the year. Mortgage rates are near current multi-decade highs, limiting purchasing power and sidelining prospective buyers. Unless financing conditions improve meaningfully, housing demand is likely to remain restrained, resulting in slower sales and weak prices. As of September, median existing-home price was $325,000, softening slightly from August’s $330,000 and unchanged from a year ago. Nationally, seasonally unadjusted existing home sales were down 3.9 percent YoY, a second consecutive month of sales declines, while YTD sales volumes remained slightly ahead of last year’s pace. National median price reached $422,700, maintaining a steady growth pace at about 1.4 percent YoY. September’s new-home sales in U.S. declined 3.4 percent YoY. As of the third quarter, YTD new-home sales were 2.9 percent below last year’s pace. Inventory turnover was slow at 15 percent, down from 16.2 percent a year ago. At this pace, fewer than two in ten existing homes (1.5 homes) on the market went under contract during the month. The median seller price cut remained similar to a year ago at $15,000, equivalent to roughly 4.5 percent of the initial listing price. As of September, active inventory is at a 5.7-month supply, similar to a year ago. The unsold inventory has an average DoM of 98 days, compared to a DoM of 65 days among the sold. items.description: New Home Market Update Zonda tracks 85% of the production new home market across the United States. Given the proprietary database, Zonda is uniquely positioned to capture trends and changes in the new home market. This report showcases the latest housing trends in the new home market for October 2026. November 20, 2026 – 5 min read Table of Content: The new home market has slipped into underperformance October marked another step backward for the new home market. Sales declined 3.1% month-over-month and 11.7% year-over-year, a considerably steeper annual decline than September's 4.6% drop. The weakness was widespread, with pending sales declining year-over-year across all of Zonda's select markets. The national Zonda Market Ranking also slipped into slightly underperforming territory for the first time since December 2022. The latest figures reinforce what builders have been telling us for months. Zonda's October builder sentiment survey found that 86% of builders reported slower-than-expected demand, up from 84% in September. In their comments, builders pointed to declining traffic, limited buyer urgency, and growing frustration with the effectiveness of incentives. “One of the biggest challenges for builders right now is generating enough buyer interest in the first place,” said Sarah Bonnarens, director of economic research for Zonda and NewHomeSource. “Builders still have an advantage when it comes to pricing and financing flexibility, but those tools can only do so much when buyer traffic is down. The challenge is keeping sales moving without putting even more pressure on margins.” The annual decline in new home sales deepened Zonda's new home sales metric counts the number of new home contract sales each month and accounts for both cancellations and seasonality. This metric shows there were 638,568 new homes sold in October on a seasonally adjusted annualized rate. This was a decline of 3.1% from last month and a drop of 11.7% from a year ago. On a non-seasonally adjusted basis, 50,770 homes were sold, 11.6% lower than last year and 2.8% below the same month in 2019. Incentives remain a key feature of the new home market, helping to sustain sales activity amid ongoing affordability pressures. In October, 64% of new home communities offered incentives on to-be-built homes and 83% on quick move-in supply. Note, these are only publicly available incentives so they will underrepresent overall usage. All select markets saw PSI fall YOY Zonda's New Home Pending Sales Index (PSI) was created to help account for fluctuations in supply by combining both total sales volume with the average sales rate per month per community. The October PSI came in at 122.8, representing an 11.4% decline from the same month last year. The index is currently 29.5% below cycle highs. On a month-over-month basis, seasonally adjusted new home sales decreased 1.9%. The markets that held up the best relative to last year were Minneapolis (-0.3%), Charlotte (-1.1%), and Tampa (-3.5%). Minneapolis was down compared to the last year but grew 10.2% month-over-month. Inversely, the metros that performed the worst year-over-year were Los Angeles/OC (-31.4%), Riverside/San Bernardino (-28.4%), and Denver (-26.3%). On a monthly basis, Minneapolis, Sacramento, and Denver were the best performing markets. The National ZMR dropped to slightly underperforming In order to add further context to sales, Zonda created the Zonda Market Ranking (ZMR). The ZMR accounts for both sales pace and volume, is seasonally adjusted, and is taken as a percentage relative to a baseline market average. Based on the percentage above or below baseline, markets are bucketed into performance groups ranging from significantly underperforming to significantly overperforming relative to historical activity. The map below shows a snapshot of top production markets by region. Zonda also offers the ZMR for entry-level, move-up/move-down, and high-end markets. Subscribers of the National Outlook report can access all top markets and the tiered breakdown in Zonda’s portal. Non-subscribers can access the tiered maps for the select 10 markets by clicking below. Zonda’s snapshot markets were split between 0% overperforming, 10% average, and 90% underperforming. Among Zonda’s top 55 major markets, 5% were overperforming , 25% were average , and 70% were underperforming . Importantly, the ZMR does not account for what it takes to sell a home. For example, securing a sale might still feel difficult in a significantly overperforming market, but if the incentives offered result in a sale, we count the sale. items.description: How Much of a Pay Raise Would Today's Renters Need to Afford a Home? Demetria C. Lester November 13, 2026 Seeking a more suburban lifestyle—with the additional space, yard, and private garage often found in a single-family home—does not necessarily require stretching the budget to buy. For most families, buying is a significant financial stretch. A household that can comfortably afford rent on a single-family home would need a $14,408 pay increase to cover the monthly costs of owning one, even before setting aside money for a down payment. Across the country, the typical rent for a single-family home is $2,243 per month, compared with $2,603 per month to own one with a 20% down payment—a difference of $360 each month. Using the common guideline of spending no more than 30% of household income on housing, a household needs to earn $89,724 to comfortably afford rent and $104,132 to buy. For many households, renting a house is a deliberate choice, not a fallback. It requires less income than ownership and leaves more room in the monthly budget. The income increase required to buy a home is now the largest since early 2025, exceeding twice the $6,463 needed in February 2026, when mortgage rates briefly dipped below 6%. The difference varies considerably by market. It is greatest in San Jose, where the income needed to buy ($404,925) is more than twice the income needed to rent ($190,561)—a gap of $214,364. San Francisco has the next-largest gap at $139,353, followed by San Diego ($84,101), New York ($78,208) and Los Angeles ($78,003). The smallest annual differences are in Pittsburgh ($2,554), Houston ($4,500) and Cincinnati ($4,774). Buffalo is the only market where buying would not require an income increase. Even after securing that increase, prospective buyers face another challenge: saving for a 20% down payment. According to Zillow’s 2026 Consumer Housing Trends Report, about 30% of mortgage buyers receive a gift or loan from family or friends, while 46% rely on at least two sources, including down payment assistance programs. Beyond monthly expenses, households weighing renting against buying should consider purchase-related upfront costs, the potential to build equity and renters’ option to invest the money they would otherwise use for a down payment. Zillow’s rent-versus-buy analysis estimates the national break-even point—the time an owner must stay in a home for buying to become more advantageous than renting—at 7.8 years with a 20% down payment. As renting a house becomes an increasingly attractive value, more people are choosing to rent. Nationwide rental demand has risen 22.1% year over year, according to the Zillow Observed Renter Demand Index (ZORDI). Demand for single-family rentals is up 24.3%, about twice the 12.1% increase for multifamily rentals. Demand increased most in San Jose, where ZORDI is 78.9% higher than a year ago. San Francisco followed at 60.5%, then Austin at 59.6%, Miami at 51.5% and Jacksonville at 47.9%. San Jose and San Francisco are also among the markets where homebuying is least attainable and rents are climbing rapidly, rising 8.9% and 12.2%, respectively. Rent growth is more modest in Austin, Miami and Jacksonville, at 1.1%, 2.1% and 2.6%, respectively. Some markets are bucking the national trend. ZORDI has declined year over year in Providence (-4.3%), Richmond (-1.9%), Baltimore (-1.7%), Hartford (-1.3%) and Washington, D.C. (-0.9%). items.title: Are NIMBY concerns about new apartments valid?
items.description: Are NIMBY concerns about new apartments valid? by Chuck Ehmann Posted November 20, 2026 in Market Research I recently saw an announcement that a new mixed-use apartment development would be built at a busy intersection in the heart of Dallas and immediately after began seeing the NIMBY posts about it on social media. The usual suspects were there: increased traffic (on an already heavily traveled street?), potential crime, noise, decreased property values, etc. Are there real concerns or is it reactionary? I asked a few AI tools if their concerns were valid and their consensus was “a little bit yes but mostly no”. Granted, a new residential development will add some vehicle trips locally, but apartments generate fewer vehicle trips than single-family homes if they are located near jobs, retail and transit. Modern apartment developers are cognizant of traffic levels and patterns and should design their access, ingress and egress to mitigate the issue. Local congestion can still get worse at a particular intersection or on a narrow street, especially in car-dependent areas but walkable access to retail, restaurants and services can reduce the concern. Additionally, modern transportation research shows that traditional traffic models often overstate vehicle trips for multifamily housing, particularly in urban or mixed-use environments. Crime is probably the most researched concern, and the evidence is largely inconsistent with the claim that new apartment developments inherently increase crime. Crime is strongly related to neighborhood conditions and more associated with older, dysfunctional apartment communities with poor maintenance, weak management and usually nonexistent security. Some studies have found that neighborhoods with high concentrations of rental housing have higher crime rates, but that does not prove that new apartments cause crime. Rental housing is often located in denser, lower-income, or more commercially active areas where crime rates already differ. More recent research discovered that increasing housing investment and homeownership generally correlated with lower crime, particularly in economically healthy cities. Construction noise is real and temporary. Permanent noise depends on site design, balconies, parking access, trash collection, outdoor amenities and the surrounding road network. Density itself does not automatically create excessive noise, but poorly designed projects can increase neighbor complaints and privacy problems. As to property values, the evidence is mixed, but newer, well-designed multifamily developments generally do not produce the large property-value declines often predicted by nearby residents. Effects depend heavily on project quality, neighborhood conditions and whether the project replaces a vacant or underutilized site. Additionally, other studies find new apartments lower or hold down nearby rents for existing apartments as supply increases and properties compete for residents. One issue not mentioned this time was schools, but school impacts are typically small because apartments house fewer children per unit. The bottom line is that for multifamily development specifically, the research generally finds that traffic impacts are real but measurable, while claims about crime and neighborhood decline are largely unsupported when researchers isolate the effect of the new housing from the characteristics of the neighborhood where it is built. Good design, traffic mitigation and parking and management standards can address those issues more directly than blocking the project does. items.description: State-Level Employment Situation: October 2026 November 20, 2026 Danushka Nanayakkara-Skillington No Comments The labor market showed signs of improvement in October following a modest growth in September. However, construction employment recorded a modest decline, highlighting ongoing challenges in the residential construction sector. In October, nonfarm payroll employment increased in 37 states and the District of Columbia (D.C.) compared to September, while 11 states recorded declines. Minnesota and Vermont reported no change. According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics , total U.S. nonfarm payroll employment increased by 165,000 jobs in October , following a gain of 60,000 jobs in September. Through October, monthly payroll gains have averaged 86,000 jobs per month for this year based on the current data vintage. On a month-over-month basis, employment gains were led by California (+47,100), followed by Texas (+30,600) and Indiana (+15,900). In contrast, the 11 states that recorded losses collectively shed 25,300 jobs, with New York posting the largest decline (-6,600). In percentage terms, Indiana and Kansas recorded the strongest increase (+0.5%), while West Virginia and Colorado experienced the largest decrease (-0.2%) between September and October. Over the 12 months ending in October, total nonfarm employment increased by 885,000 jobs nationwide, representing a 0.6% gain. Job gains ranged from 700 in Rhode Island to 203,300 in Texas. Collectively, five states and D.C. lost 25,700 jobs over the past 12 months, with Virginia recording the largest decline (-9,700). Hawaii reported no change during this 12-month period. In percentage terms, job growth ranged from 0.1% in New Jersey, Oregon, and Rhode Island to 2.0% in Louisiana. New York and Hawaii reported no change over the past 12 months. Among states experiencing employment declines, losses ranged from 0.1% in Vermont to 0.7% in Montana. D.C., however, recorded a steeper decline of 1.2%. Construction Employment Construction employment 1 —which includes both residential and non-residential construction, posted a net loss in October. Twenty-nine states added construction jobs compared to September, while 15 states lost jobs; six states and D.C. reported no change. Texas recorded the largest monthly gain (+6,900), while New York recorded the largest loss (-6,100). Overall, the construction sector lost a net 3,000 jobs nationwide in October. In percentage terms, Delaware recorded the strongest monthly increase (+2.4%), while Montana experienced the steepest decline (-2.4%). Year-over-year, construction employment increased by 124,000 jobs nationwide, a 1.5% gain from October 2025. Texas led all states with an increase of 26,900 construction jobs, while Georgia recorded the largest loss (-6,300). In percentage terms, Louisiana posted the strongest annual growth in construction employment (+13.0%), while West Virginia experienced the largest decline (-4.5%). State Unemployment Rate The state unemployment rate is a key indicator of labor market conditions, measuring the share of the labor force that is actively seeking work but unable to find employment. Higher unemployment rates generally signal weaker economic conditions, while lower rates indicate tighter labor markets that may contribute to upward wage pressures. South Dakota recorded the nation's lowest unemployment rate at 2.0%, while D.C. posted the highest rate at 5.4%. The elevated unemployment rate in D.C. reflects significant federal workforce reductions and layoffs that occurred during 2025. North Dakota, New Hampshire, Vermont, Hawaii, and Nebraska also reported unemployment rates of 3.0% or below. Meanwhile, Michigan, California, and Connecticut recorded unemployment rates of 5.0% or higher. For this analysis, BLS combined employment totals for mining, logging, and construction are treated as construction employment for the District of Columbia, Delaware, and Hawaii. items.description: Read more CNBC personal finance coverage How to get Anthropic stock — without buying the IPO There's a growing 'property tax revolt' as homeowners face rising costs Congress passes bill to protect older investors from financial fraud CNBC's Financial Advisor 100: Best financial advisors, top firms for 2026 ranked CNBC Elite Advisors: Top ultra-high net worth wealth management firms for 2026 The push, which revives a longstanding mortgage industry request, also comes several weeks after President Donald Trump issued an executive order that included calling for the launch of a federal pilot program that would cancel mortgage insurance on certain conventional loans once borrowers meet equity requirements. The order would apply generally to future loans backed by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac — two government-sponsored enterprises that purchase qualifying mortgages from lenders and resell them as bundled securities. It wouldn't apply to FHA loans. Here's who uses FHA mortgages FHA mortgages are issued by private lenders but insured by the federal government, which protects lenders against losses if a borrower defaults. The loans are designed to make homeownership more accessible, particularly for borrowers with limited savings for a down payment or with lower credit scores. Affordability challenges persist in the housing market, with elevated home prices and mortgage rates putting homeownership out of reach for many prospective buyers. Existing homeowners are also facing rising costs alongside their mortgages, including property taxes and homeowners insurance amid overall high inflation . About 83% of new FHA purchase loans went to first-time homebuyers in the most recent fiscal year, according to the FHA report to Congress. Altogether, the FHA insured more than 8.4 million mortgages as of Sept. 30. The median age of first-time buyers is 40, according to a new report from the National Association of Realtors. watch now VIDEO 0:31 00:31 Can you afford to buy a home? Personal Finance FHA loans also require borrowers to pay mortgage insurance regardless of the size of their down payment. Under current rules established in 2013 , FHA borrowers with a down payment that's less than 10% of the loan must pay mortgage insurance premiums for the duration of the loan. Those who put 10% or more down pay that insurance for 11 years. Borrowers generally pay both an upfront mortgage insurance premium and an annual premium, which is typically divided into monthly payments. The upfront premium is usually 1.75% of the base loan amount and can be financed into the mortgage. For many borrowers with 30-year FHA loans, the annual premium is 0.55% of the outstanding loan balance. Conventional mortgages generally don't require mortgage insurance unless the loan is for more than 80% of the home's value. In 2022, the premium typically ranged from 0.58% to 1.86% annually, according to Fannie Mae . If those borrowers have to pay mortgage insurance, they can typically request its removal once they've built 20% equity in the home, or it is automatically canceled when their loan drops to 78% of the original value. Proposals from the mortgage industry The mortgage industry has floated two different proposals. One would reduce the rate that applies to FHA mortgage insurance. For example, the Mortgage Bankers Association recently suggested a rate reduction of 20 basis points , which would lower the standard 0.55% rate to 0.35% for new borrowers. For example: On a $350,000 mortgage, a 0.55% rate generally translates into $1,925 annually, or about $160 monthly, at the start of the loan. As the principal owed slowly goes down over time through a borrower's monthly payments, so does that mortgage insurance amount. At 0.35%, the annual premium would be $1,225 at the start of the loan, or $102 monthly — a difference of $58 per month. The FHA last cut that rate in 2023 , when it was reduced from 0.85%. At the time, HUD estimated that affected borrowers would save an average of $800 annually. However, in the FHA's new report to Congress, the agency noted that the 2023 cut has reduced the fund's revenue, contributing to a decline in its capital ratio. The other industry proposal would implement auto-cancellation of premiums once the loan balance fell to 78% of the home's original value at purchase — in other words, the same as for Fannie- and Freddie-backed mortgages. Cancellation prevents the squeeze for borrowers who have paid down their loans and shouldn't be paying for coverage they have outgrown. Michael Farrell National Association of Mortgage Brokers "Cancellation prevents the squeeze for borrowers who have paid down their loans and shouldn't be paying for coverage they have outgrown," said Michael Farrell, president of the National Association of Mortgage Brokers, a trade group that generally has supported the cancellation proposal. "NAMB believes that cancellation at 78% protects the [FHA insurance fund], because premiums can restart if the [capital] ratio ever falls to 2%," Farrell said. FHA mortgages received that treatment from 2001 through 2013, but the agency eliminated it to shore up its insurance fund after financial reserves deteriorated over time following the housing market crash, which led to the 2008 financial crisis. Whether the proposals will go anywhere this time is uncertain. HUD, which oversees the FHA, did not respond to a CNBC email seeking more information. items.title: Beyond the Rent: In an era of tech outages, here’s how apartment firms can prepare their networks
items.description: Beyond the Rent: In an era of tech outages, here’s how apartment firms can prepare their networks Former CISA Director Chris Krebs told OPTECH attendees that they need to know which AI tools employees and vendors are using. Published Nov. 20, 2026 Leslie Shaver Senior Reporter Share Copy link Email LinkedIn X/Twitter Facebook Print License Add us on Google Chris Krebs speaks at OPTECH 2026 on Nov. 17. Les Shaver/Multifamily Dive Beyond the Rent is Multifamily Dive’s analysis of the trends driving supply, demand and operations in the apartment industry. You can read the previous edition here . The Real Estate Technology & Transformation Center picked a helluva time to hold OPTECH 2026, which ran from Nov. 16 to 18 at the MGM Grand Hotel & Casino in Las Vegas. In the week before the conference began, a Microsoft 365 outage disrupted Outlook , angering users worldwide (including this one). The next day, the Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop, while Workday also had a much less high-profile outage that day. For people like me who don’t like getting on planes (it’s not about crashing; it's about not having control, as I often tell my wife), the ground stop was alarming. The week of OPTECH, outages followed at JPMorgan Chase, Apple, the National Security Agency and, to my chagrin, briefly, United. That one led to a minor freakout as I walked the OPTECH expo floor. My apologies to those of you who chose to speak with me. In an extremely fortunate bit of planning, RETTC actually booked former United States Director of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency Chris Krebs to speak on Tuesday. It wasn’t surprising to learn that he tore up his original presentation to focus on current events. With the FAA having a hardware-related shutdown, Krebs’ explanation for the majority of the disruptions was that artificial intelligence is helping firms find software flaws. As they scramble to patch issues, outages occur. “We're going to have more outages,” Krebs said. “But I also think we're going to learn from every one of these. So there are always lessons learned, whether it's from the Chase, United [and] from Microsoft.” However, he emphasized this won’t be a short-term process. “The good news is we're almost done, right?” Krebs said. “Nope. We're in like the second inning of this ball game.” How apartment firms can fortify their systems For apartment firms looking to protect their own systems, Krebs said the first place to start is by peeking under the hood and seeing what’s happening in their own companies. Find out what AI tools employees are using. “You have a pretty significant risk at that point of a PII [personally identifiable information] or other sensitive data leak,” Krebs said. “So you've got to be very cognizant of any sort of AI use in your environment, what it touches, including the secrets, the keys that it has access to. That can get out, and then you've got a completely different problem with a data breach.” Apartment firms also need to know who inside the organization owns the problem if something goes wrong and where the kill switch is. If “it's either misbehaving or the vendor is a jerk, and I want to turn it off, how do I do that?” Krebs said. Suppliers also deserve scrutiny, according to Krebs. “You're going to have to extend that review and analysis to your vendors because every one of your vendors is probably using AI, and I'm not quite sure if they're telling you,” he said. “So, vendors in the room, be transparent.” Above all, companies that develop their own products need to know their exposure and quickly patch any issues, which is reportedly happening across the broader economy right now. “If you do develop code, and a lot of you do for some of your proprietary products, make sure that you're using AI to scan the code that's being developed,” Krebs said. “Now, don't just grab some random open source model. There are specific harnesses and products that are developed specifically for secure coding.” Krebs’ points struck a chord with me. In the midst of the chaos, it may be a good time for apartment executives to look at their own systems and determine what happens if there’s an outage. While I can’t control United’s schedule from the OPTECH exhibition floor (in case you’re wondering, I made my flight and am writing this final paragraph from the friendly skies above Champaign, Illinois), multifamily leaders can prepare for what’s coming. items.description: Federal Reserve announces College Fed Challenge winners For release at 4:15 p.m. EST Share --> --> --> --> --> --> The University of California, Los Angeles won the 23rd Annual National College Fed Challenge. ' data-gallery='global-photo' data-toggle="lightbox"> The University of California, Los Angeles won the 23rd Annual National College Fed Challenge. The University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) won the 23rd annual national College Fed Challenge on Friday, a team competition that encourages undergraduate students to learn about the U.S. economy, monetary policymaking, and the role of the Federal Reserve System. Teams analyze economic and financial conditions and formulate a monetary policy recommendation, modeling the Federal Open Market Committee. The team, from Los Angeles, California, represented the San Francisco District and included Aarushi Maheshwari, Annika Chan, Atul Prasanth, Caitlyn Cox, Finn Karish, Eli Brooks (alternate), Kennedy Yang (alternate), Manasi Vartak (alternate), Ronojoy Borpujari (alternate), and Sahil Sudani (alternate). The team's advisers were Chris Surro and Ali Haider Ismail. "I am very happy to congratulate the students who competed in this year's College Fed Challenge, especially the winners and finalists," said Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh. "They took on the same big questions we policymakers face. I'm impressed by their talent, their rigor, and their eagerness to think hard about monetary policy and the economy." This year's College Fed Challenge included 141 schools from 34 states across the nation, the most in the competition's history. Teams submitted video presentations or participated in local competitions last month. Twenty-one semi-finalist teams then participated in question-and-answer sessions held earlier this month, and seven finalists were invited to the Federal Reserve Board for the national finals. The other national finalists were the University of Chicago in second place and the University of Maryland, College Park in third place. Teams with honorable mentions include Cleveland State University, Harvard College, Pennsylvania State University, and St. Lawrence University. Teams were evaluated on their economic analysis, responses to the judges' questions, teamwork, and presentations. For media inquiries, please email [email protected] or call 202-452-2955. items.description: Closings decrease 21% in Houston by Emily Marek November 20, 2026 The Houston Weekly Activity Snapshot from the Houston Association of REALTORS. Closed home sales fell 21% year over year in Houston during the week ended Nov. 16, according to the Weekly Activity Snapshot from the Houston Association of REALTORS® . Buyers purchased 1,115 properties, down from 1,412 during the same week in 2025. Pending listings also decreased annually, with 1,477 properties going under contract, down from 1,979 a year prior. That was a decline of 25.3%. New listings declined, albeit more modestly: Sellers added 3,169 properties to the market, down 2.3% year over year. Meanwhile, property showings, listing views on HAR.com and open houses all declined annually as well, by 10.1%, 9.7% and 1.3%, respectively. items.title: Everyday Economics: The federal government delayed the housing recovery – The Center Square
items.description: Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Houses line a suburban neighborhood. Photo: Alan Wooten / The Center Square Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save (The Center Square) – Existing-home sales fell in October to their slowest pace since August 2010, according to the National Association of Realtors . Federal policy is pulling in two directions: HUD has cut lenders’ costs on taxpayer-backed FHA loans, while tariffs, the conflict with Iran and federal borrowing add to the inflation and interest-rate pressures that keep mortgages expensive. According to Freddie Mac , the 30-year fixed rate has been climbing since the war began and now exceeds year ago levels. According to the National Association of Realtors , October existing-home sales fell to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.75 million, the weakest pace since August 2010, and 8.8% below a year earlier. According to my calculations using NAR’s unadjusted data , actual October closings fell 11.7%, partly because October had one fewer business day than last year. The unadjusted annual decline deepened sharply from September’s 4.2%. The year started better than those figures suggest. According to the same calculations, 3.4 million homes sold through October, just 0.6% fewer than during the same period in 2025. My October housing report , based on Redfin data, found that seasonally adjusted pending sales fell 3.6% from September to their lowest level since April 2020. The same report found that active listings increased even though fewer sellers listed, because homes are selling more slowly. The problem is still affordability. My report calculated that monthly principal and interest on the median-priced home reached $2,137 with 20% down, up 11.2% from a year earlier. By my calculation, higher rates added approximately $223 to the monthly payment, while a slightly lower Redfin median sale price saved about $7. HUD has targeted a different cost: making the loan. According to HUD , June changes streamlined FHA appraisal-review requirements and eliminated a duplicative homebuyer disclosure form. HUD estimates the appraisal change alone saves lenders about $425 per review, or roughly $3.3 million a year industrywide. HUD’s announcement does not say how much of those savings will reach borrowers. The Appraisal Institute has said eliminating long-standing review requirements raises questions about oversight of collateral on FHA loans, which the federal government insures, American Banker reported . Any savings from lower origination costs are expected to be small next to the roughly $223 a month that higher rates added to the typical payment. Other federal policies affect what borrowers pay each month. According to Federal Reserve Bank of New York researchers , tariffs raise prices for imported and domestically produced goods. According to the Energy Information Administration , attacks on tankers, constrained shipping and falling inventories pushed oil prices higher again in October. Federal borrowing matters, too. According to the Congressional Budget Office , growing government debt crowds out private investment and contributes to higher interest rates. My analysis found that sticky inflation and worries about U.S. fiscal sustainability have pushed long-term Treasury yields higher, and mortgage rates track those long-term yields far more closely than the Federal Reserve’s policy rate. Producer prices are still rising. According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), producer prices rose 6.5% over the year through October, their largest increase since November 2022. BLS reported that truck freight prices rose 3.9% in October, accounting for more than 80% of the increase in services prices, even as diesel prices fell 7.9% from September. Truck freight prices were up 24.6% from a year earlier, according to BLS. According to my analysis of BLS producer price data, retail margins narrowed for computers, appliances and sporting goods, consistent with shoppers resisting higher prices. This week’s retail sales report could help clarify how spending is holding up. Retail sales and builder confidence arrive Tuesday, followed by housing starts and permits Wednesday. Orphe Divounguy, PhD, is chief economist for The Center Square and founder and chief economist of Quantitative Research Group, the co-host of the Everyday Economics podcast and a former economist at Zillow. He has briefed the White House Council of Economic Advisers, testified before state legislatures, and delivers more than 30 speaking engagements annually. Orphe also has a large media footprint, typically 300-400 media mentions per quarter. He specializes in housing, labor markets, and the broader economy. items.title: The Blue Wave Has Foreign Capital Dipping Its Toes Back Into U.S. Commercial Real Estate
items.description: Trade wars , inflation and prolonged conflict in the Middle East made foreign investors increasingly cautious about the U.S., even as cross-border transactions rebounded globally. But in the aftermath of Democratic Party victories in midterm elections across the country, overseas capital may once again be warming to American real estate, fund managers said at Bisnow ’s New York City State of the Market event on Thursday. Unsplash/Amelia “The sentiment toward the U.S. was very, very negative, and even since two weeks ago, we've seen some thawing in those pools of capital that were pulling back from the U.S. for the past couple of years,” Vistria Group partner Sherry Wang said onstage. That marks a sharp reversal from earlier this year, when Wang said some foreign funds rescinded mandates to invest in the U.S., citing geopolitical concerns even as they continued to “believe in the underlying real estate for the most part.” In the first half of the year, cross-border investment in commercial real estate surged 56% to $71.8B globally, Reuters reported . Most of that increase came from Asia and Europe. Singapore ranked first among individual markets, attracting $8.7B in investment. The U.S. captured a smaller-than-usual slice of the global market. In the 12 months leading up to September, the country attracted $28B, a 15% share of all cross-border investment, according to a report by Colliers . That lagged below its five-year average of nearly 19%. Between 2022 and 2024, many investors held allocations in the U.S. steady, before decreasing their targets by 10 basis points in 2025, according to the Association of Foreign Investors in Real Estate . In an AFIRE survey conducted throughout July and August, 53% of respondents, representing more than $4T in global assets, said they plan to decrease or not change their overall U.S. allocations. That’s even though 58% of those same respondents had a positive view of the U.S. economy. Those with a negative outlook more than doubled from the same time last year, from 12.5% to nearly 27%, with more than 90% of respondents citing the U.S. political landscape as the reason why. In its first survey since the midterms , Oxford Economics found that U.S. consumer sentiment rose and year-ahead inflation expectations fell by a full percentage point to 3.7%, the most substantial decline since the start of the Iran war . Having a blue Congress and a red White House is likely to create new hurdles that block laws, budgets or appointments from approval. For the real estate industry, that may not be such a bad thing, Legal 1031 Exchange President Todd Pajonas said during the event, held at Convene One Liberty Plaza. “There's not going to be any change to the tax code, which drives a lot of business. There's not going to be huge swings in monetary policy. We're not going to see the huge tariffs . We're going to see an end, hopefully, to the conflict in the Middle East because there's not going to be the political will to do it,” Pajonas said. “I think the next two years are going to look somewhat better because of political gridlock.” AFIRE CEO Gunnar Branson told GlobeSt earlier this month that his members expressed a similar sentiment to him on the day of the election. Real estate played a prominent role in November’s election, with housing affordability and data center backlash taking center stage. Across the country, a series of Republican stronghold states flipped, including Texas, Georgia, Ohio, Iowa and Alaska, in some cases giving Democrats control for the first time in decades . Foreign investors may take a moment to recalibrate, but they are unlikely to be dissuaded in the long run, panelists said. “I don't think there's any foreign capital that has redlined, crossed off New York because of the political climate,” NAI Global Senior Managing Director and Head of Capital Markets Arthur Milston said. “In fact, I think most people view that typically as transient.” Manhattan’s median rent reached $5,279 per month in October, up 6% year-over-year, while vacancy fell to 1.3%, the lowest level since March 2020, according to Corcoran . The city has led the country in office recovery and is one of the few markets where new office supply is being delivered. items.title: U.S. concession use falls again, but the depth of discount is the deepest in 15 years
items.description: U.S. concession use falls again, but the depth of discount is the deepest in 15 years by Meggan Taylor Posted November 19, 2026 in Rent Growth Rate U.S. apartment concession use fell for a fifth consecutive month in October 2026, while the average discount reached its deepest level in more than 15 years. Concessions were offered on 13.1% of stabilized U.S. units, down 1.4 points from September 2026 and the lowest reading since June 2025, according to data from Realpage Market Analytics . The October decline was the deepest of the five monthly decreases and the deepest the market has seen since March 2025. The timing makes the October 2026 decline particularly notable. Concession use increased from September to October in 15 of the previous 16 years, making this month's decline a departure from the typical seasonal pattern. Meanwhile, the average concession increased modestly to 11.2%, the deepest discount in data going back to January 2010. At 11.2%, the typical incentive equals about 5.8 weeks free on a 12-month lease. Usage falls fastest in Class A and B stock Concession usage fell in every product class in October 2026, led by Class B and Class A units. Class B usage dropped 1.8 points to 11.3%, marking a fifth straight monthly decline and the asset’s lowest reading since March 2025. Similarly, Class A fell 1.5 points to 11%, its lowest level since September 2023. However, Class C usage slipped only 0.3 points to 17.7%, so the gap between Class C and Class A concessions widened to 6.7 points. Usage also fell in all four floorplans for a fifth straight month, with declines ranging from 1.3 to 1.7 points. Efficiencies posted the deepest of those declines yet remained the floorplan with the highest concession use, at 15.4% of units. One-bedroom, two-bedroom and three-bedroom units saw usage closer to 12% and 13%. However, widespread narrowing in concession use is only half of the October 2026 story. Concession depth gets deeper despite lower usage While fewer units across the U.S. carried a concession, the size of the discount kept getting deeper. The average U.S. concession was 11.2% in October 2026, showing relief in only two months since March 2024, when the discount was 7.5%. That pattern is consistent with operators trimming the number of units that carry an incentive before trimming the incentive itself. Class C posted the largest increase of the three classes in October 2026, up 0.4 points to 11.5%, its deepest average concession since March 2010. Class B discounts increased modestly to 10.8% and Class A discounts softened to 11.4%. Across floorplans, average discounts ranged from 10.9% for three-bedroom units to 12.2% for efficiencies. Before 2026, the average concession last reached 11% in March 2010, in the aftermath of the Great Financial Crisis. Discount depth then was nearly identical to October 2026’s 11.2%, but reach was not. Operators were discounting 50.0% of stabilized units in March 2010, against 13.1% now, so today’s incentives reach roughly a quarter as many units. Looking ahead Five consecutive months of declining concession use, including an October drop that ran against typical seasonal patterns, point to operators offering concessions on a smaller share of units. At the same time, discount depth reached its highest level in more than 15 years. The coming winter months will be a key test: concession use typically rises from October through February, so continued declines through the off-season would signal that reliance on incentives is easing beyond normal seasonal patterns. items.description: Townhouse Construction Declining November 20, 2026 Robert Dietz No Comments Third quarter 2026 data reveal declining conditions for townhouse construction as housing affordability challenges affect homebuyer demand, particularly in larger metropolitan markets. According to NAHB analysis of the most recent Census data of Starts and Completions by Purpose and Design, during the third quarter of 2026, single-family attached starts totaled 40,000, down 14% from the third quarter of 2025. Over the last four quarters, townhouse construction starts totaled 154,000 homes, down 13% from the prior four quarter period (179,000). Townhouses made up 17% of all of single-family housing starts for the third quarter of the year. Using a one-year moving average, the market share fell back to 17%, after reaching an all time high in the third quarter of 2025 (18.7%). Prior to the current cycle, the peak market share of the last two decades for townhouse construction was set during the first quarter of 2008, when the percentage reached 14.6% on a one-year moving average basis. This high point was set after a fairly consistent increase in the share beginning in the early 1990s. The long-run prospects for townhouse construction remain positive given growing numbers of homebuyers looking for medium-density residential neighborhoods , such as urban villages that offer walkable environments and other amenities.
